extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / introductory proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Defines and develops equivalence relations, equivalence classes, partitions, integers modulo n, and the set-theoretic definition of functions; includes key theorems, examples, and exercises for undergraduate discrete math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes these three properties as the defining criteria (example: = on a set). It shows how to check each property on examples and uses them repeatedly in proofs (e.g., Theorem 11.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A and any a ∈ A, the equivalence class containing a is the subset {x ∈ A : xRa}, denoted [a].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate computing [a] for finite sets, polynomials (by degree), and congruence modulo n; exercises ask to list classes for specific relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: [a] = [b] iff aRb (characterization of classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A and a,b ∈ A, [a] = [b] if and only if aRb (Theorem 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties; the result allows switching between class-equality and the relation aRb and is used to deduce many class identities (e.g., [−3]=[9] when −3≡9 (mod 3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes form a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: The set {[a] : a ∈ A} of equivalence classes of R forms a partition of A (Theorem 11.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit criteria: (1) union of all [a] equals A because each x∈A lies in [x], and (2) if [a] ≠ [b] then [a] ∩ [b] = ∅ (proved by contrapositive). Examples and exercises reinforce checking these two conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition of a set A is a set of non-empty subsets of A such that the union of all subsets equals A, and the intersection of any two different subsets is ∅ (Definition 11.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives multiple partitions of small finite sets as examples; partitions are described as 'dividing up' A into pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition ↔ equivalence relation correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every equivalence relation on A yields a partition of A (its classes), and conversely any partition P of A defines an equivalence relation R where xRy iff x and y belong to the same block in P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondence is stated explicitly after Theorem 11.2 and reinforced by Exercise 4 of Section 11.3; this is a standard two-way characterization used throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: For n ∈ N, the relation ≡ (mod n) on Z is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, hence an equivalence relation (Example 11.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text works out the equivalence classes for n=3 and n=5 explicitly ([0], [1], ...), shows there are exactly n classes [0]..[n−1], and demonstrates how these classes partition Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing equivalence classes in examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalence classes can be described concretely in context: e.g., polynomials grouped by degree; congruence classes as residue classes; parity/sign classes on small finite sets (Figure 11.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how to compute and name classes ([3x^2+2] = {ax^2+bx+c : a ≠ 0}) and how to read classes off diagrams; warns some equivalence relations (equality on R) are too large to draw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of equivalence relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If R and S are equivalence relations on A then R ∩ S is also an equivalence relation (Exercise 10; illustrated by R2 ∩ R3 = R4 in Figure 11.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a method to combine relations while preserving equivalence properties; text suggests checking reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity on intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of equivalence relations may fail
rubrics_metrics.description: R ∪ S need not be an equivalence relation in general (Exercise 12 asks to prove or disprove that R ∪ S is an equivalence relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a caution: reflexivity may hold but transitivity or symmetry can fail under union; readers are prompted to construct counterexamples or proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest equivalence relation containing R (equivalence closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a reflexive symmetric relation R on a finite set A, define S by xSy iff there is a finite chain xRx1, x1Rx2, ..., xnRy; then S is an equivalence relation and R ⊆ S; S is the unique smallest equivalence relation containing R (Exercise 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the idea of taking the transitive/symmetric/reflexive closure (connectedness via R-chains) to produce an equivalence relation; useful when producing equivalence relations from raw relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation class-count facts for finite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is an equivalence relation on a finite set A and every equivalence class has the same cardinality m, then |R| can be expressed in terms of m and |A| (Exercise 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages counting techniques: number of classes = |A|/m, etc.; useful for combinatorial verification of partitions/classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation from A to B (generalized relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation from a set A to a set B is a subset R ⊆ A × B; the notation (x,y)∈R is abbreviated xRy (Definition 11.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text distinguishes relations on a single set from relations between two different sets (e.g., ∈ is a relation from elements to subsets); diagrams for relations A→B draw two labeled node-sets with arrows from A to B (Figure 11.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a special relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f from A to B is a relation f ⊆ A × B such that for each a ∈ A the relation f contains exactly one ordered pair of form (a,b) (Definition 12.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, vertical line test in familiar graph sense; functions are treated as sets (graphs) and can be visualized by ordered pairs or arrow diagrams; examples demonstrate functions that map multiple domain elements to same codomain element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, and range
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B, A is the domain, B is the codomain, and the range is {f(a) : a ∈ A} = {b : (a,b) ∈ f} (Definition 12.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The range is always a subset of the codomain; examples show range may be proper subset (e.g., f(n)=|n|+2 has range {2,3,4,...}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of operations on equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining operations [a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a]·[b]=[ab] on equivalence classes (e.g., in Z_n), one must verify these definitions are independent of representative choices (consistency/well-definedness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives a proof using congruence: if [a]=[a'] and [b]=[b'] then a≡a'(mod n), b≡b'(mod n) imply ab≡a'b'(mod n), so [ab]=[a'b']; exercises ask to check addition similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integers modulo n (Z_n) structure and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Z_n is the set {[0],[1],...,[n−1]} of equivalence classes mod n; define [a]+[b]=[a+b], [a]·[b]=[ab]; Z_n has n elements and satisfies commutativity of + and · and distributive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include addition/multiplication tables for n=5; text emphasizes Z_n is a small number system and notes how to interpret results (e.g., [2]+[3]=[5]=[0]). Exercises ask to build tables for other n and to check ring-like properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and equality of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions are equal as sets if they have the same ordered pairs; two functions f:A→B and g:A→D are equal if f(x)=g(x) for every x∈A (Definition 12.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal functions must have the same domain; codomains may differ even if functions are equal pointwise (example f:(Z→N) and g:(Z→Z) with same rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function domain as Cartesian-product input notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If domain is a Cartesian product A×B, one writes f(m,n) for f((m,n)) for notational convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text remarks this is a common shorthand; examples include ϕ(m,n)=6m−9n mapping Z^2→Z and shows how to determine its range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining range by algebraic argument
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the range of a function given by a formula, show all outputs satisfy a property and then find inputs that realize any value with that property (Example: ϕ(m,n)=6m−9n has range = multiples of 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates a two-step method: show range ⊆ desired set, then for each element of desired set find preimage; useful rubric for students solving range problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual representations of relations and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams differ for relations on a single set (nodes and arrows, possibly loops) vs relations from A to B (two labeled collections of nodes with arrows from A to B); arrow diagrams are especially convenient for finite/generic sets (Figures 11.2, 11.3, 12.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns some relations (e.g., equality on R) are too large to draw; recommends arrow diagrams for finite examples and conventional graphs for numeric functions.
